data.title: Rifampicin
data.summary: Antileprosy drugs · Rifamycin (semisynthetic antibiotic); antileprosy and antituberculous
data.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** Rifamycin (semisynthetic antibiotic); antileprosy and antituberculous

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (β-subunit, rpoB gene) → no RNA synthesis → bactericidal
- Most potent bactericidal drug against M. leprae — a single 600 mg dose kills over 99.9% of viable bacilli
- Resistance from rpoB mutations — never used as monotherapy

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed on an empty stomach; widely distributed (CSF, tissues, secretions)
- Metabolised in the liver; excreted in bile (enterohepatic circulation)
- Potent inducer of CYP3A4, 2C9, 2C19 and P-gp — induces its own metabolism

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Leprosy: part of MDT (monthly supervised dose); single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts
- Tuberculosis including cutaneous TB (HRZE regimen)
- Atypical mycobacteria (M. marinum, M. ulcerans), rhinoscleroma, cutaneous leishmaniasis (limited)
- Hidradenitis suppurativa: clindamycin 300 mg + rifampicin 300 mg twice daily for 10–12 weeks
- Recurrent staphylococcal furunculosis (decolonisation, with another antibiotic)
- Pruritus of cholestasis (pregnancy excluded), brucellosis

## Dose & formulations
- Leprosy MDT: 600 mg once a month (supervised); children 10–14 years 450 mg; under 10 years 10 mg/kg
- TB: 10 mg/kg/day (max 600 mg) in fixed-dose combinations
- Take on an empty stomach (1 h before or 2 h after food)

## Adverse effects
- Orange-red discolouration of urine, sweat, tears (stains soft contact lenses)
- Hepatotoxicity (more with isoniazid and in alcoholics)
- Intermittent dosing: 'flu-like syndrome', thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia, acute renal failure (immune-mediated)
- Rash, pruritus, flushing; rarely SJS/TEN, DRESS

## Contraindications
- Jaundice; hypersensitivity
- Concurrent protease inhibitors (except with rifabutin substitution) and some other ART

## Drug interactions
- Powerful enzyme inducer — reduces levels of: oral contraceptives (use another method), corticosteroids (double steroid dose in lepra reactions/ENL), cyclosporine, tacrolimus, azoles (itraconazole, voriconazole), warfarin, sulfonylureas, methadone, digoxin, dapsone, PIs, nevirapine, dolutegravir (needs 50 mg twice daily)
- Hepatotoxicity increased with isoniazid, pyrazinamide, alcohol

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline and if symptoms; CBC on intermittent dosing
- Review all co-prescribed drugs

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used in pregnancy for leprosy and TB; vitamin K to the newborn (risk of haemorrhagic disease) when given in late pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Single monthly dose kills >99.9% of M. leprae
- Enzyme inducer — OCP failure and need to double steroid dose
- Orange-red body fluids
- Flu-like syndrome with intermittent dosing

_Sources: Khopkar ch.6 and ch.7; Wolverton 4e ch.9 (rifamycins) and ch.66 (Drug interactions). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
